key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of M. F., a Child
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed dismissal of a father's petition, holding that under OCGA 15-11-244(c) a change in a parent's circumstances sufficient to make a previously unfit parent fit can be a material change in the child's circumstances warranting modification, vacatur or revocation of a permanent guardianship.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Georgia rule for reopening a permanent guardianship entered as the permanency outcome.
key_cases.quote: We hold only that a change in parental circumstances sufficient to render a previously unfit parent fit may constitute a material change in the circumstances of the child.

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of K. M., a Child
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that a juvenile court deciding a parent's petition to end a third party's temporary guardianship must apply the clear and convincing evidence standard for physical or significant long-term emotional harm, not a probable-cause standard, and that the burden rests on the third party seeking to keep custody.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the standard and burden for dissolving a kinship guardianship and returning the child to a parent.
key_cases.quote: the burden of satisfying this stringent standard rests on the third party who is seeking to obtain or maintain custody of the child

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of D. L. T.
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed placement of two siblings in the Department's permanent custody with their foster family rather than with paternal grandparents, holding that after termination there is no conclusive relative preference and the juvenile court has wide discretion to weigh the children's best interests, including their sibling bond.
key_cases.relevance: It governs the choice between kinship permanency and adoption by a foster family after termination.
key_cases.quote: Following the termination of parental rights, juvenile courts are not obligated to attempt to place a child with relatives, but need only consider the best interests of the child.

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed, holding that a caregiver who had received parental power by a valid relinquishment contract and stood in loco parentis was entitled to the notice, hearing and juvenile-code safeguards that the juvenile court denied her before the child was removed and custody given to the agency.
key_cases.relevance: It recognizes in loco parentis custody as a durable permanency status the juvenile court must respect.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court failed to acknowledge the appellant's rights, and undoubtedly failed to provide her with the safeguards and procedures of the juvenile code

key_cases.case_name: Drummond v. Fulton County Department of Family & Children Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed dismissal of long-term foster parents' suit to block removal of their foster child, holding that foster parents acquire no legal right to the child, no right to adopt over the agency's withheld consent, and no Fourteenth Amendment property or liberty interest from the foster relationship.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a psychological-parent relationship does not by itself create permanency rights in Georgia.
key_cases.quote: foster parents have no right to adopt a foster child and thus no right to contest the agency's withholding of consent

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed and remanded two grandparent-versus-parent custody cases, upholding the best-interest standard of OCGA 19-7-1(b.1) as constitutional only under a narrowing construction requiring the third party first to prove by clear and convincing evidence that parental custody would harm the child, and only then that third-party custody would best promote the child's welfare and happiness.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the constitutional floor for any kinship or third-party permanency arrangement in Georgia: harm to the child, proved by clear and convincing evidence, not a bare comparison of homes.
key_cases.quote: the third party must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the child will suffer physical or emotional harm if custody were awarded to the biological parent
